concepts.title: Geological Structure and the Himalayan Mountains
concepts.definition: India's physiography rests on the Peninsular block, the Himalayas and other young fold mountains, and the Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra plain; the Himalayas show three major divisions of Greater Himalaya or Himadri, Lesser Himalaya or Himachal and Shiwaliks, along with Purvanchal eastern hills.
concepts.key_idea: The syntaxial bends at Nanga Parvat and Namcha Barwa and the trans-Himalayan Karakoram, Ladakh and Zanskar ranges complete the northern mountain wall.

concepts.title: Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau and Coastal Regions
concepts.definition: The Northern Plains formed of alluvium stretch from Punjab to Assam with Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar belts; the Peninsular Plateau carries the Deccan trap, Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau, and the coastal plains with Keralan backwaters, plus islands of Andaman-Nicobar and Lakshadweep, complete the physiographic divisions.
concepts.key_idea: The plateau's structural differences, the Gondwana coal fields and the volcanic Deccan traps mark the peninsular block's distinct geological history.

concepts.title: Significance of the Himalayas and Physiographic Diversity
concepts.definition: The Himalayan barrier shields the plains from cold winds, forces monsoon rains to ascend and feed perennial rivers, and together with the plateau, plains, coasts and islands gives India unmatched physiographic diversity of landscapes, soils, climates and economies.
concepts.key_idea: Physiographic regions guide agriculture, industry and settlement, since each division offers distinct resources like alluvial soils of the plains and minerals of the plateau.
